summary: This informational document describes the challenges of running protocols efficiently on constrained, battery-powered devices, and practices used to cope. It summarizes the main link-layer techniques for saving energy and highlights how they affect higher-layer protocols. It is aimed at protocol designers working on Internet of Things systems.

plainLanguage.summary: Small gadgets run on tiny batteries, so they must nap a lot. This explains tricks that let them nap and still talk to the network.

questions: how do iot protocols save energy
subtitle: Making wireless protocols work on battery-powered devices.

tldr.problem: Battery-powered IoT devices need to communicate, but wireless communication is expensive: listening for messages can consume as much power as transmitting.
tldr.mechanism: By duty-cycling the radio (turning it off most of the time) and designing protocols with awareness of lower-layer constraints, devices can extend battery life from hours or days to months or years.
tldr.outcome: This RFC summarizes energy-saving techniques at every layer of the IETF protocol stack for constrained devices, helping protocol designers achieve efficiency across CoAP, RPL, 6LoWPAN and other technologies.

today: RFC 8352 is an Informational RFC describing practices that remain standard in constrained-node networks. The energy-efficient protocols and techniques it describes (CoAP, 6LoWPAN, RPL) are widely deployed in commercial IoT systems.

sections.title: Energy Challenges in IoT
sections.content:
Battery-powered and energy-harvesting devices are the heart of Internet of Things systems such as environmental monitoring and sensor networks. These constrained devices need to communicate efficiently because replacing batteries in thousands of deployed sensors is impractical. The IETF has developed lightweight protocols like IPv6 over Low-Power Wireless Personal Area Networks (6LoWPAN), the IPv6 Routing Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks (RPL), and the Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP) to enable such devices to participate in the Internet with minimal power consumption.

Achieving energy efficiency requires awareness of how each layer of the protocol stack affects power consumption. Unlike traditional networks where transmission and reception are relatively inexpensive compared to processing, in constrained IoT devices the radio interface is the dominant power consumer.
sections.plainLanguage: When you have thousands of tiny devices running on batteries, you cannot change the batteries often, so they need to be very power-efficient.

sections.title: Radio Duty Cycling
sections.content:
The most significant power consumer is idle listening: keeping the radio on to receive messages even when none are coming. To address this, devices use radio duty cycling (RDC), turning the radio off most of the time and waking it up periodically to check for incoming data. By comparison, listening for 1000 milliseconds can consume 63,000 microjoules of energy on a typical sensor device, whereas a single transmission costs only 96 to 1790 microjoules depending on whether the receiver is awake.

Three main RDC techniques dominate: Channel sampling, where the radio wakes frequently to detect activity; scheduled transmissions, like Bluetooth LE, where both sides agree on when to communicate; and listen-after-send, where a node stays in sleep mode by default and polls for pending data. Duty cycling trades off latency and throughput for energy savings: a sleepy device may have to wait longer to receive messages.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of always listening, devices nap and check for messages on a schedule, like checking your mailbox once a day instead of staring at it all day.

sections.title: The Lightweight Protocol Stack
sections.content:
Constrained-node networks use a lightweight Internet protocol stack tailored for low-power operation. At the link layer, technologies like IEEE 802.15.4, Bluetooth LE, and DECT ULE provide duty-cycling mechanisms. The 6LoWPAN adaptation layer solves the mismatch between IPv6 (which expects 1280-octet packets) and low-power radios (which may support only 127 octets), using fragmentation and header compression to reduce overhead. IPv6 runs on top, with energy-aware neighbor discovery via 6LoWPAN-ND.

At the routing layer, RPL is optimized for the common many-to-one pattern where sensor nodes send data toward a border router. RPL uses the Trickle algorithm to minimize control-plane messages, which can be tuned to balance energy consumption against network convergence time.
sections.plainLanguage: The network stack is redesigned for tiny devices: headers get squashed down, the radio naps on a schedule, and routers send fewer control messages.

sections.title: Application-Layer Efficiency
sections.content:
CoAP (Constrained Application Protocol) was designed with energy constraints in mind. Unlike HTTP, which uses a chatty request-response model, CoAP uses a compact 4-byte binary header and supports an observe mode where a client subscribes to resource updates instead of polling repeatedly. This lets an energy-constrained server sleep between notifications. CoAP also supports caching through proxies, so requests for sleepy servers can be answered from cached copies, and data aggregation reduces the number of transmissions needed.

CoAP timers require careful tuning: the default retransmission timeout (RTO) starts at 2 to 3 seconds, but link-layer duty cycling may introduce much longer latencies. Protocols should also consider data compression before encryption, since encryption destroys redundancy that compression relies on.
sections.plainLanguage: CoAP is a lightweight email protocol: devices register interest in updates instead of asking repeatedly, and they can cache answers from other devices.

sections.title: Cross-Layer Awareness
sections.content:
Energy efficiency emerges from cooperation across layers. The RFC emphasizes that upper-layer protocols must be aware of lower-layer constraints. For example, protocols should synchronize with the parameters of the link layer: if the radio wakes every 30 seconds, sending keep-alives every 5 seconds wastes energy. Similarly, Neighbor Unreachability Detection (NUD) timeouts in IPv6 are too aggressive for duty-cycled links and should be relaxed.

Broadcast and non-synchronized transmissions are especially costly because they require the radio to stay awake longer to guarantee reception. Where possible, aggregating multiple messages into a single transmission (packet bundling) or using synchronized communication reduces power consumption. The RFC concludes that energy-efficient design is not about any single technique but about making every layer aware of the constraints of the layers below.
sections.plainLanguage: Every layer of the network needs to know what the lower layers are doing, so they do not waste energy asking or sending things when the radio is asleep.
